month.title: Convert capability into options
month.theme: Turn a year of evidence into a portfolio, a story and real opportunities, then decide the next bet.
month.mastery: Defend your Year 1 Capability Report with evidence.
month.checkpoint: Portfolio published, GitHub tidy, applications or client conversations under way, and a Year 1 report that answers what you can now build.

weeks.title: Portfolio
weeks.objective: Show increasing capability: five proofs that tell one story.
learn: Portfolio as argument: design + technology + AI + product
Case study structure: problem, evidence, decisions, result
Showing your role honestly
Visual design of the portfolio itself
Writing for skimmers and for readers
Linking to live work and code
Getting critique
practice: Fill all five Portfolio slots in this platform
Write the capstone case study in its final form
Get critique from one product person and one engineer
Cut anything that doesn't support the story

build.title: Published portfolio
build.brief: A published portfolio site presenting your five capability proofs with case studies, live links and code links.

weeks.prove: A stranger can say what you can build, and how you think, after 3 minutes on the site.
reflect: What story does your portfolio tell that your CV doesn't?

tryFirst.task: Write the 3-sentence introduction for your portfolio home page.
tryFirst.hint: Who you are, what you build, and the evidence. No adjectives.
tryFirst.explanation: Specific claims backed by visible work beat 'passionate designer'. Name the combination that makes you rare, and point to the proof.
tryFirst.solution: 'I'm a product designer who builds. Over the last year I've shipped five working products, from accessible interfaces to an AI brief-extractor with evaluation, and a capstone used by 20+ local businesses. I work best where design, code and AI meet a real business problem.'

weeks.title: GitHub and technical proof
weeks.objective: Make your code speak for you: clean repositories, clear READMEs, visible history.
learn: What reviewers look for in a GitHub profile
README structure: what, why, screenshot, how to run, architecture, learnings
The profile README
Pinning the right repositories
Commit history as evidence of process
Licences, and what to keep private
Removing secrets and personal data before publishing
practice: Audit every repository: keep, polish or archive
Add architecture diagrams to your top 3 repositories
Scan for secrets and personal data

build.title: GitHub profile as technical proof
build.brief: A tidy GitHub profile: a profile README, 4–6 pinned repositories with strong READMEs, diagrams and live links, and nothing sensitive.

weeks.prove: Ask an engineer to review one repository for 10 minutes, and act on their feedback.
reflect: Which repository are you proudest of technically, and why?

tryFirst.task: Write the README outline for your capstone repository.
tryFirst.hint: Think about two readers: someone who wants to try it in 30 seconds, and an engineer deciding whether you can build.
tryFirst.explanation: A README is the front door. Lead with what it is and a screenshot, then how to run it, then how it works and what you learned.
tryFirst.solution:
# Project name: one-line description
![screenshot]
Live: link · Case study: link
## Why it exists (the problem in 2–3 lines)
## Run it locally
## How it works (diagram + stack)
## Decisions and trade-offs (link the ADRs)
## Testing and evaluation
## What I'd do next

weeks.title: Career applications / opportunities
weeks.objective: Turn evidence into conversations (applications, clients, opportunities) without risking the floor.
learn: Targeting roles that compound: design engineer, product designer who codes, AI product builder, founding designer
Tailoring applications to your evidence
Technical interviews for hybrid roles
Freelance positioning and pricing
Networking without cringe: ask for advice, show your work
Evaluating offers: pay, learning, stability, runway
Protect the floor: no resignation without a signed offer and runway
practice: Shortlist 15 roles or clients that match your evidence
Do 2 mock interviews explaining your capstone
Log every experiment in the Career section

build.title: Opportunity pipeline
build.brief: At least 10 logged career experiments (applications, proposals, conversations), each with a status and what you learned, and career targets updated based on the responses.

weeks.prove: Explain your capstone in a mock technical interview, including what broke and what you'd change.
reflect: What does the market's response say about your evidence?
weeks.ship: Applications sent and the pipeline tracked.

tryFirst.task: A job asks for 'React, TypeScript, design systems, AI features'. Write the 4-line evidence block for your application.
tryFirst.hint: Map each requirement to a specific project and a link, not to adjectives.
tryFirst.explanation: Hiring managers look for proof. One line per requirement, each pointing to something they can open, beats a paragraph of claims.
tryFirst.solution:
React + TypeScript: habit tracker and capstone, strict TS, tested core flow (link)
Design systems: tokens and components in Figma and in code for the capstone (link)
AI features: brief extractor with structured output, 20-case evaluation and review flow (link)
Product: capstone used by 20+ businesses, 3 shipped iterations (case study link)

weeks.title: Annual review
weeks.objective: Look at the whole year's evidence and decide the next bet deliberately.
learn: Reviewing evidence, not feelings
Capability compounding: what can you do now that you couldn't before?
Choosing what to deepen and what to abandon
Writing a thesis for Year 2
Financial runway and the next level of risk
Sustainable pace
Celebrating without inflating
practice: Generate the Year 1 Capability Report in this platform
Re-read all your weekly reviews and highlight patterns
Compare your earning power now with a year ago
Write the Year 2 thesis in one paragraph

build.title: Year 1 Capability Report
build.brief: Complete the Year 1 Capability Report: what you can build, explain and ship; what broke; what you learned; the opportunities you discovered; your earning power; and the Year 2 thesis.

weeks.prove: Mastery test: defend your Year 1 Capability Report with evidence.
reflect: What should you bet on next, and what evidence says so?
weeks.ship: Capability Report exported or printed, and shared with one trusted person.

tryFirst.task: Write your Year 2 thesis in three sentences.
tryFirst.hint: What you'll bet on, why the evidence supports it, and how you'll protect the floor while doing it.
tryFirst.explanation: A thesis is a falsifiable bet: it names a direction, the evidence behind it, and the conditions under which you would change course.
tryFirst.solution: 'In Year 2 I'll go deep on AI product engineering for Indian SMB workflows, because my strongest evidence (capstone usage, interview pull) is there. I'll keep a stable role while running two paid experiments, and I'll only go full-time on a product after 6 months of runway and 10 paying customers.'

resources.title: Paul Graham · How to do great work

mastery.title: Defend your Year 1 Capability Report
mastery.challenge: Present your Year 1 Capability Report to someone whose judgment you trust, and defend each claim with evidence.
constraints: Every capability claim links to a build, a mastery test or a published artefact
criteria: Answers what you can build, explain and ship now
What broke, and what you learned from it
Opportunities discovered, with the strongest one's evidence
Change in earning power, honestly assessed
What to deepen, and what to abandon
A Year 2 thesis with a plan to protect the floor
